_meta.note: Conservative, general first-aid guidance consistent with widely-published public first-aid education (e.g. Red Cross / WHO style lay-person guidance). This is NOT a substitute for a certified first-aid/CPR course, and has not been reviewed by a licensed clinician for this project. No drug names, no dosages, no invasive procedures. If in doubt in a real situation, call emergency services first and follow their instructions.

topics.summary: Firm direct pressure controls most severe bleeding until help arrives.
immediate_steps: Call emergency services (or have someone else call) right away.
Apply firm, direct pressure on the wound with a clean cloth, bandage, or your hand.
Keep steady pressure on — do not lift the cloth to check, add more layers on top if it soaks through.
If possible, raise the injured area above the level of the heart.
Keep the person still, warm, and lying down if they feel faint.
avoid: Do not remove any object that is embedded in the wound.
Do not remove the cloth once pressure is applied — add more on top instead.
Do not apply a tourniquet unless you are trained to use one and bleeding cannot be controlled any other way.
when_to_call_emergency: Bleeding that won't stop or slow with firm pressure
Spurting or pooling blood
The person becomes pale, faint, confused, or loses consciousness
topics.source: General public first-aid education (Red Cross / WHO style guidance)

topics.summary: Cool the burn with running water; don't use ice, butter, or ointments.
immediate_steps: Move the person away from the source of the burn.
Cool the burn under cool (not ice-cold) running water for 10-20 minutes.
Remove tight clothing or jewelry near the burn before it swells, unless it's stuck to the skin.
Cover loosely with a clean, non-fluffy cloth or cling film.
Keep the person warm and comfortable while cooling the burn.
avoid: Do not apply ice directly, butter, oil, or toothpaste to a burn.
Do not pop any blisters.
Do not pull off clothing that is stuck to the burned skin.
when_to_call_emergency: Large burns, or a burn on the face, hands, feet, groin, or a major joint
Deep burns (white, leathery, or charred-looking skin)
Burns from chemicals, electricity, or fire in an enclosed space
The person is a young child, elderly, or has trouble breathing
topics.source: General public first-aid education (Red Cross / WHO style guidance)

topics.summary: Encourage coughing first; escalate to back blows and abdominal thrusts if the airway stays blocked.
immediate_steps: If the person can cough or speak, encourage them to keep coughing — don't intervene yet.
If they cannot cough, speak, or breathe: call emergency services immediately.
Lean the person forward and give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
If that doesn't clear it, and you are trained, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver).
Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object is cleared or emergency help arrives.
If the person becomes unconscious, lower them to the ground and begin CPR if you are trained, and ensure emergency services are on the way.
avoid: Do not do abdominal thrusts on infants under 1 year — use back blows and chest thrusts instead, and get trained guidance before attempting this on an infant.
Do not perform abdominal thrusts if you have not been shown how — call for emergency help and continue back blows.
Do not put your fingers blindly into the mouth to try to grab the object.
when_to_call_emergency: The person cannot breathe, cough, or make sound
Lips or face start turning blue
The obstruction does not clear after first-aid attempts
The person loses consciousness
topics.source: General public first-aid education (Red Cross / WHO style guidance)

topics.summary: Lay the person down and raise their legs; most fainting resolves within a minute.
immediate_steps: Help the person lie down flat and raise their legs about 12 inches (30 cm) if possible.
Loosen any tight clothing around the neck.
Check that they are breathing normally.
Once they come around, have them rest lying down for a few minutes before sitting up slowly.
Give water once they are fully alert, if they can swallow safely.
avoid: Do not sit the person up or stand them up quickly.
Do not give food or water while they are still drowsy or not fully alert.
Do not leave them alone until they've fully recovered.
when_to_call_emergency: They don't regain consciousness within about a minute
They were injured in a fall
Fainting is accompanied by chest pain, irregular heartbeat, confusion, or difficulty breathing
It happens repeatedly, or during pregnancy
topics.source: General public first-aid education (Red Cross / WHO style guidance)

topics.summary: Protect from injury, cushion the head, and time it — most seizures stop on their own within a couple of minutes.
immediate_steps: Stay calm and stay with the person for the whole seizure.
Clear the area of anything hard or sharp they could hit.
Cushion their head with something soft.
Time the seizure from when it starts.
Once the jerking stops, gently roll them onto their side (recovery position) and check breathing.
Stay with them until they are fully alert, and speak calmly and reassuringly as they come around.
avoid: Do not hold the person down or try to stop their movements.
Do not put anything in their mouth — they cannot swallow their tongue, and this can cause injury.
Do not give food, water, or anything by mouth until they are fully alert.
when_to_call_emergency: The seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes
A second seizure starts soon after the first
The person does not regain consciousness or normal breathing afterward
It's their first-ever seizure, it happened in water, or they are pregnant or injured
topics.source: General public first-aid education (Red Cross / WHO style guidance)

topics.summary: Use FAST — Face, Arms, Speech, Time. Call emergency services immediately if any sign is present.
immediate_steps: Check FAST: Face — does one side droop when they smile? Arms — can they raise both arms evenly? Speech — is it slurred or strange?
If any of these signs are present, call emergency services immediately — Time matters, note when symptoms started.
Keep the person still, calm, and comfortable while waiting for help.
If they are unconscious but breathing, place them in the recovery position on their side.
avoid: Do not give them food, water, or any medication.
Do not let them drive themselves or wait to 'see if it passes' — treat it as a time-critical emergency.
Do not delay calling for help to see if symptoms improve.
when_to_call_emergency: Any single FAST sign is present, even if it resolves
Sudden numbness or weakness, especially on one side
Sudden confusion, trouble speaking or understanding speech
Sudden severe headache with no known cause
topics.source: General public first-aid education (Red Cross / WHO style guidance)

topics.summary: Call emergency services immediately; use an epinephrine auto-injector right away if the person has one.
immediate_steps: Call emergency services immediately.
If the person has their own prescribed epinephrine auto-injector, help them use it right away, following the device's own instructions.
Help them into a comfortable position — lying flat with legs raised is often recommended, unless they're having trouble breathing, in which case let them sit up.
Stay with them and monitor breathing and consciousness until help arrives.

A second dose of epinephrine (from a second auto-injector, if available) may be needed if there's no improvement after several minutes — follow the device instructions or emergency dispatcher's guidance.
avoid: Do not wait to see if symptoms improve on their own before calling for help.
Do not have them stand or walk around.
Do not give anything by mouth if they are having trouble breathing or swallowing.
when_to_call_emergency: Swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat
Difficulty breathing or wheezing
Widespread hives with dizziness or a feeling of impending doom
Any reaction after a known allergen exposure that's worsening quickly
topics.source: General public first-aid education (Red Cross / WHO style guidance)
